title: Cumulative Review 3: Modules 1 to 9
intro: Spaced review mixes questions from earlier modules. Retrieving older material now is what makes it stick. Items you miss come back for a retry round.

items.q: Researchers survey 300 volunteers who responded to a flyer in a gym about exercise habits. A reporter concludes that most adults exercise regularly. The main problem is
o: The volunteer sample may not represent all adults, so the statistic may miss the parameter
Exercise is measured on a nominal scale
items.why: Gym volunteers are likely more active than the general population. A biased sample produces error that a larger sample would not fix.

items.q: The null hypothesis for a related-samples t is
o: The mean difference in the population is zero
The two sample means are equal

items.q: The t statistic is a ratio of
o: The obtained mean difference to the estimated standard error
items.why: It is how many estimated standard errors the sample mean is from the hypothesized mean.

items.q: Which sample mean is more surprising if the population mean is 100 and sigma is 15?
items.why: With n = 36, SE = 2.5 and z = 3.2. With n = 9, SE = 5 and z = 1.6. The same difference is more surprising with a larger sample.

items.q: Cohen's d for a related-samples t is commonly computed as
o: Mean difference divided by the SD of the difference scores
Mean difference divided by the standard error
Mean difference divided by the sample mean
items.why: It expresses the average change in units of the standard deviation of the changes.

items.q: A researcher tests whether a program changes test scores in a population with mean 75 and sigma 12. A sample of 36 has M = 79. The z is 2.00. At alpha = .05 two-tailed, what is the decision?
o: Reject the null, since 2.00 exceeds the critical value of 1.96
Retain the null, since 2.00 is small
The decision depends on the effect size
items.why: The critical values at alpha = .05 two-tailed are plus and minus 1.96. The test statistic falls in the critical region.

items.q: A larger difference between sample means, with all else equal, will
items.why: The mean difference is the numerator of t.

o: A sample mean with a hypothesized population mean
items.why: It is used when the population mean is known or hypothesized but sigma is not.

items.q: Degrees of freedom for a related-samples t test are
o: n minus 1, where n is the number of pairs or difference scores
items.why: df depends on the number of difference scores.

items.q: A researcher says, "My correlation was r = −.45, so something went wrong because the effect should be positive." What is the best reply?
o: A negative r is not an error. It means one variable tends to go down as the other goes up
The sign does not matter at all
Take the absolute value and ignore the direction
items.why: The sign tells you the direction. A negative correlation can be perfectly meaningful, for example more practice and fewer errors.

o: Separate groups of participants in each condition
The same participants in each condition
items.why: Different people provide the scores in each condition, so the scores are independent.

items.q: Eight response times (seconds) are 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, and 40. The mean is 8.5 and the median is 4.5. Which summary describes a typical response best?
o: The median, because one extreme score pulls the mean upward
The mean, because it uses every score
The mode, because it is largest
Neither, because the data are nominal
items.why: The score of 40 distorts the mean. The median stays near where most responses fall.

items.q: Random assignment of participants to two groups helps ensure that
o: The groups are comparable before treatment, supporting causal inference
The samples are representative of the population
items.why: It controls for pre-existing differences on average, which is what gives the design its causal leverage.

items.q: If a 95 percent CI for the mean difference includes the null value, the two-tailed test at alpha = .05
items.why: The CI and the test agree. A null value inside the interval is a plausible value.

items.q: Scores on a scale have mean 50 and SD 10 and are normally distributed. About what proportion score below 45?
items.why: z = (45 minus 50)/10 = −0.50. The tail beyond z = 0.50 is .3085.
